description: Pop Art answers the consumer society head-on. **Warhol** and **Lichtenstein** turn advertising, comic books and movie stars into high art.

hero.hook: A soup can, a comic-strip panel: what if the ordinary was the icon of the century?

blocks.text: **Pop Art**, from the mid-**1950s** to the **1970s**, answered the [[American consumer society of the 1950s-60s]] and its mass culture. Advertising, comic books, Hollywood stars: everything became material for art.

With **Andy Warhol** and **Roy Lichtenstein**, the wall between the museum and the supermarket came down. The everyday object became an icon. The value of the artwork and the role of the artist were both turned upside down.

Pop Art was born in **Great Britain** with the [[Independent Group]], but it exploded in the **United States** in the **1960s**. Postwar wealth, supermarkets, logos everywhere: the visual landscape of American life had changed.
In 1957, Richard Hamilton defined Pop Art with a list of adjectives: “ephemeral”, “cheap”, “sexy”. Art to be consumed as fast as a magazine.

The pop artists set themselves against [[Abstract Expressionism]], the inward-looking canvases that dominated the scene. When Warhol painted soup cans, he showed that people define themselves by what they buy. Repetition drains the image of its emotion and leaves only its selling power.

sections.title: From the everyday to the museum

blocks.text: **Andy Warhol** (1928-1987), a former advertising illustrator, applied industrial methods to art. His **Factory** in New York was no longer a lonely sanctuary: assistants and friends produced the work together.

blocks.caption: Marilyn in series: the star as a reproducible product

blocks.text: Warhol filled more than 600 “time capsules”: boxes where he dumped letters, bills and even leftover food.

His favorite technique was [[Screen printing]], which let him copy one image dozens of times. By multiplying Marilyn Monroe, he showed the idea of [[Aura and mechanized reproduction (Walter Benjamin)]]: the more an image circulates, the less “sacred” it is, and the more it becomes an icon. Fame itself is a product.

sections.title: Warhol: the studio as a factory

blocks.text: **Roy Lichtenstein** (1923-1997) went after the language of **comics**. He isolated a single panel loaded with emotional cliché and painted it on a monumental scale.

blocks.caption: Ben-Day dots painted by hand: the factory imitated by a brushstroke

blocks.text: To judge a composition, Lichtenstein looked at his canvases upside down in a mirror, to see whether they held together as pure abstraction.

His signature was the [[Ben-Day]] dot, those tiny industrial printing dots that create shading. He painted them by hand with a stencil: hours of work to imitate what a machine does in seconds. *Whaam!* turned a throwaway comic panel into modern history painting.

sections.title: Lichtenstein: the comic strip blown up

blocks.text: Pop Art changed both the market and the institutions. The artist's brand counts as much as the brushwork. In **2022**, a Warhol portrait of Marilyn reached **195 million** dollars: the mass image, made sacred, became the most valuable object of all.

blocks.text: Warhol's prediction about “15 minutes of fame” has become our daily digital life. Memes and recycled images come straight from that revolution.
Pop Art broke the barrier between high art and mass culture. Through screen printing and Ben-Day dots, Warhol and Lichtenstein turned everyday objects and movie stars into lasting icons.
